column1: What actually computes an embedding vector when SQL requests embedding generation?
column2:
The embedding model.
SQL calls the model and can store the returned vector.
Review source

column1: Which SQL columns are good candidates for text embedding input?
column2:
Meaningful text, such as titles and descriptions.
Choose fields that describe the content users need to retrieve.
Review source

column1: Why usually exclude IDs, numeric values, and operational metadata from embeddings?
column2:
They usually add little semantic meaning while consuming tokens.
Keep these values as ordinary relational data rather than embedding them by default.
Review source

column1: Why can overly large text chunks reduce similarity-search precision?
column2:
They can combine unrelated ideas in one embedding.
Keep each chunk focused on related content.
Review source

column1: What must you check after character-based chunking before sending chunks to an embedding model?
column2:
Each chunk's token count against the model's input limit.
A character count does not guarantee a particular token count.
Review source

column1: Why define chunking rules near the source tables in SQL?
column2:
To adjust splitting behavior without rewriting application-side splitting logic.
Change the chunking arguments in the SQL query.
Review source

column1: Why store vectors in a separate embeddings table?
column2:
To rebuild embeddings independently of the original source data.
A dedicated table also makes vector storage usage easier to track.
Review source

column1: What value links each generated text chunk back to its source document?
column2:
The source document's ID.
Carry the document ID forward when the query expands a row into several chunks.
Review source

column1: Why can FIXED chunking require extra care to preserve meaning?
column2:
A character-based split can cut through a word or sentence.
Fixed sizing does not guarantee semantic boundaries.
Review source

column1: What does each output row from AI_GENERATE_CHUNKS represent?
column2:
One text chunk from the source value.
A document can produce multiple rows because the function returns a table.
